provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall types of chemical bonds, balance chemical equations and solve simple stoichiometry problems.

Introduction:
Last term we studied chemical bonding and reactions. Today we will revise these key concepts to strengthen our foundation for this term's work.

Content:
Chemical bonding involves ionic, covalent and metallic bonds. Ionic bonding occurs between metals and non-metals like sodium chloride in our cooking salt. Covalent bonding happens between non-metals like in water which we drink daily. Chemical equations must balance atoms on both sides. For example, the reaction of hydrogen with oxygen to form water is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Stoichiometry uses mole calculations to determine quantities in reactions like how much baking soda is needed to neutralize stomach acid.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to balance five equations and identify the types of bonds in given compounds.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding?
2. Balance the equation: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O
3. Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to burn 10g of methane.
4. Give one example of each type of bond found in Nigerian households.

Summary:
Today's revision has reinforced our understanding of chemical bonding and equations which are fundamental to our chemistry studies.

topics.title: Atomic structure
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to write electron configurations, identify isotopes and calculate relative atomic masses.

Introduction:
We have previously learned about atoms as the basic units of matter. Today we will explore their structure in greater detail, focusing on electron arrangement and isotopes.

Content:
Electron configuration describes how electrons are distributed in an atom's shells. For example, sodium (Na) has configuration 2,8,1. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, like carbon-12 and carbon-14. The relative atomic mass is a weighted average of an element's isotopes. For instance, chlorine has two main isotopes (Cl-35 and Cl-37) with abundances of 75% and 25% respectively, giving a relative atomic mass of 35.5. In Nigeria, some isotopes are used in medical imaging and agriculture research.

Class activity:
Students will complete a table of electron configurations for the first 20 elements and identify isotopes among given examples.

Evaluation questions:
1. Write the electron configuration of potassium.
2. Define the term isotope.
3. Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium if it has isotopes with masses 24 (78.99%) and 25 (10%) and 26 (11.01%).
4. Why do isotopes have the same chemical properties but different physical properties?

Summary:
Understanding atomic structure and isotopes is essential for explaining many chemical phenomena and applications in our daily lives.

topics.title: Periodic table
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify periodic trends, classify elements into groups and explain the significance of the periodic table.

Introduction:
Building on our knowledge of atomic structure, we now examine how elements are organized in the periodic table and the patterns that emerge.

Content:
The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number and similar properties. Periodic trends include atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity. Atomic radius decreases across a period but increases down a group. For example, lithium (Group 1) is larger than fluorine (Group 17) in the same period. Ionization energy generally increases across a period. Groups contain elements with similar valence electron configurations. Group 1 metals like sodium react vigorously with water, similar to potassium. In Nigeria, elements like gold, tantalum and columbite are economically important and found in specific regions.

Class activity:
Students will plot graphs of atomic radius versus atomic number for the third period and identify elements with similar properties in different groups.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain why atomic radius decreases across a period.
2. Compare the reactivity of lithium and fluorine.
3. Which group contains the noble gases and why are they unreactive?
4. How does the periodic table help predict chemical behavior?

Summary:
The periodic table is a powerful tool that organizes elements and reveals patterns in their properties, enabling chemists to make predictions about chemical behavior.

topics.title: Chemical bonding
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to differentiate between ionic and covalent bonding, draw Lewis structures and predict bond polarity.

Introduction:
We have previously touched on chemical bonding concepts. Today we will explore ionic and covalent bonding in detail, including their formation and properties.

Content:
Ionic bonding occurs through electron transfer between metals and non-metals, forming compounds like sodium chloride (table salt). These compounds have high melting points and conduct electricity when molten. Covalent bonding involves electron sharing between non-metals, forming molecules like water or methane. Covalent compounds generally have lower melting points and don't conduct electricity. Lewis structures represent valence electrons and bonding. For example, water has two O-H bonds with two lone pairs on oxygen. Bond polarity depends on electronegativity differences. In Nigeria, ionic compounds like alum are used in water purification, while covalent compounds form the basis of many plastics used in packaging.

Class activity:
Students will draw Lewis structures for given molecules and determine whether bonds are polar or nonpolar.

Evaluation questions:
1. Compare and contrast ionic and covalent bonding.
2. Draw the Lewis structure for carbon dioxide.
3. Why does sodium chloride conduct electricity when dissolved in water but not in solid form?
4. Predict the bond polarity in a hydrogen fluoride molecule.

Summary:
Understanding chemical bonding helps us explain the properties of substances and their behavior in reactions, which is fundamental to chemistry.

topics.title: Stoichiometry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate moles, determine empirical formulas and solve stoichiometric problems.

Introduction:
We have previously learned about chemical reactions and equations. Today we will explore how to quantify these reactions using stoichiometric calculations.

Content:
Stoichiometry involves calculations based on chemical equations using mole relationships. The mole is a unit representing 6.02 × 10^23 particles. For example, in the reaction 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, 2 moles of hydrogen react with 1 mole of oxygen to produce 2 moles of water. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance (g/mol). To solve stoichiometric problems, we convert mass to moles, use mole ratios from the equation, then convert back to mass. For instance, calculating how much oxygen is needed to burn 10g of propane involves finding moles of propane, using the 5:1 mole ratio with oxygen, then converting to oxygen mass. In Nigeria, stoichiometry is applied in industries like cement production and fertilizer manufacturing.

Class activity:
Students will solve stoichiometric problems involving limiting reactants and percentage yield using real Nigerian industrial examples.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define the mole and Avogadro's number.
2. Calculate the mass of oxygen required to burn 20g of methane completely.
3. What is a limiting reactant and how does it affect product yield?
4. If 5g of zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid to produce 0.056g of hydrogen, what is the percentage yield?

Summary:
Stoichiometric calculations enable chemists to predict quantities of reactants and products in chemical reactions, which is essential for industrial processes and laboratory work.

topics.title: Acids and bases
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define acids and bases, perform titration calculations and determine solution concentrations.

Introduction:
We have previously studied acids and bases in general terms. Today we will focus on quantitative analysis through titration and concentration calculations.

Content:
Acids are proton donors (H+ ions) while bases are proton acceptors. Titration is a technique used to determine concentration by reacting a solution of known concentration with an unknown solution. The equivalence point is reached when stoichiometrically equal amounts have reacted. For example, titrating 25.0cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration with 0.1M hydrochloric acid requires 22.5cm³ to reach the endpoint. The concentration can be calculated using MaVa = MbVb for monoprotic acids. In Nigeria, titration is used in water quality testing and in the production of local soap from palm kernel oil.

Class activity:
Students will perform a titration experiment using locally available materials like tamarind juice as an acid indicator.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define the equivalence point in a titration.
2. Calculate the concentration of NaOH if 25.0cm³ requires 30.0cm³ of 0.2M HCl for neutralization.
3. Why is phenolphthalein a suitable indicator for strong acid-strong base titrations?
4. Describe how titration is used in water quality testing in Nigeria.

Summary:
Titration is a precise analytical technique that allows us to determine concentrations of solutions, which has practical applications in various industries and quality control processes.

topics.title: Redox reactions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to assign oxidation numbers, identify redox reactions and balance redox equations.

Introduction:
We have previously studied chemical reactions in general. Today we will focus specifically on redox reactions, which involve electron transfer.

Content:
Redox reactions involve both reduction (gain of electrons) and oxidation (loss of electrons). Oxidation numbers indicate the hypothetical charge of an atom if all bonds were ionic. Rules for assigning oxidation numbers include: elements have 0, oxygen is usually -2 (except in peroxides), hydrogen is +1 with non-metals and -1 with metals. In the reaction Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu, zinc goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized) and copper from +2 to 0 (reduced). Redox reactions occur in everyday processes like rusting of iron roofs during Nigeria's harmattan season and in batteries used in torches and phones.

Class activity:
Students will assign oxidation numbers to elements in given compounds and identify redox reactions in common Nigerian scenarios like corrosion of metal objects.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer.
2. Assign oxidation numbers to all elements in KMnO4.
3. Balance the redox equation: Fe + Cl2 → FeCl3
4. Explain why rusting is a redox reaction and how it affects structures in Nigeria's coastal regions.

Summary:
Understanding redox reactions helps us explain many chemical processes, from corrosion to energy production, and is fundamental to electrochemistry.

topics.title: Electrolysis
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state Faraday's laws, predict products of electrolysis and calculate quantities in electrolysis.

Introduction:
Building on our knowledge of redox reactions, we now examine electrolysis, which uses electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous redox reactions.

Content:
Electrolysis involves passing electric current through an electrolyte to cause chemical change. Faraday's first law states that the mass of substance deposited is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed. The second law states that the masses of different substances deposited by the same quantity of electricity are proportional to their chemical equivalents. For example, in the electrolysis of molten NaCl, sodium metal and chlorine gas are produced. The amount of substance produced can be calculated using Q = It (charge = current × time) and relating to moles via Faraday's constant (96500 C/mol). In Nigeria, electrolysis is used in the production of aluminum from bauxite and in electroplating to prevent corrosion of metal objects.

Class activity:
Students will calculate the time required to deposit a certain mass of copper in an electrolytic cell using given current and conditions.

Evaluation questions:
1. State Faraday's laws of electrolysis.
2. Calculate the mass of copper deposited when a current of 2A is passed through CuSO4 solution for 30 minutes.
3. Predict the products of electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution.
4. Explain how electrolysis is used in the purification of copper in Nigeria's mining industry.

Summary:
Electrolysis is an important industrial process that uses electrical energy to drive chemical changes, with applications in metal extraction and purification.

topics.title: Energy changes
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define enthalpy, calculate enthalpy changes and explain exothermic and endothermic reactions.

Introduction:
We have previously studied chemical reactions and bonding. Today we will examine the energy changes that accompany chemical reactions, focusing on enthalpy.

Content:
Enthalpy (H) is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. Enthalpy change (ΔH) is the heat absorbed or released during a reaction. Exothermic reactions have negative ΔH values (heat released), like combustion of kerosene in stoves. Endothermic reactions have positive ΔH values (heat absorbed), like photosynthesis in plants. Enthalpy changes can be calculated using Hess's law or from standard enthalpies of formation. For example, the enthalpy of combustion of methane can be calculated from the enthalpies of formation of CO2, H2O and CH4. In Nigeria, understanding energy changes is important for fuel efficiency in transportation and for the production of local crafts like pottery which involves heating clay.

Class activity:
Students will measure temperature changes during simple reactions like dissolving ammonium nitrate in water to determine if they are exothermic or endothermic.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define enthalpy and enthalpy change.
2. Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with examples.
3. Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction: C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g) given standard enthalpies of formation.
4. Explain how energy changes affect cooking practices in Nigerian households.

Summary:
Understanding energy changes in chemical reactions helps us predict reaction feasibility and optimize processes in various applications.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve WAEC-style questions, apply chemical concepts to novel situations and manage time effectively in examinations.

Introduction:
Throughout this term, we have covered various topics in chemistry. Today we will practice WAEC examination questions to prepare for the upcoming external examinations.

Content:
WAEC chemistry questions typically test understanding of concepts rather than rote memorization. Questions may include calculations, explanations of principles, and applications to real-life situations. For example, a question might ask students to explain why aluminum pots are used for cooking in Nigeria despite aluminum being more reactive than iron. Another question might involve calculating the percentage composition of a compound like kaolin found in Nigeria. Students should practice identifying keywords in questions, applying appropriate formulas, and showing clear working in calculations. Time management is crucial, with approximately 1.8 minutes per mark in the examination.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past WAEC questions, with each group presenting solutions to specific question types.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain why sodium chloride has a high melting point.
2. Calculate the concentration of a solution prepared by dissolving 5.6g of KOH in water to make 500cm³ of solution.
3. Describe the industrial extraction of aluminum from bauxite ore.
4. Explain how the hardness of water affects soap consumption in Nigerian households.

Summary:
Regular practice of examination questions helps students become familiar with the format, improve time management, and identify areas needing further revision.
